en: The Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Most Victorious Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa for Purifying Karmic Obstructions, translated by the Tripitaka Master Divākara of India during the Great Tang Dynasty by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at the Bamboo Sprout Hermitage in Śrāvastī.
In the Jeta Grove, at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
he was together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus,
all of whom were venerable ones established in the stage of śrāvaka.
A great assembly of Arhats, well-known to all,
whose names were the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Mahākāśyapa, Aniruddha,
and other such great śrāvakas served as their leaders.
Furthermore, there was an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
all of whom dwelt in the practice of the stage of non-retrogression and were adorned with immeasurable merits.
Their names were Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
and Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Maitreya Bodhisattva,
Vijayapadmagarbha Bodhisattva,
and Sarvāvaraṇaviśodhana Bodhisattva.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva—
these thirty-two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as their leaders—
were seated together with the great assembly at that time.
Furthermore, there were ten thousand Brahmā kings,
with the Brahmā-purohita king and the Sudarśana king as their leaders.
He sat together with a multitude of Brahmās.
Furthermore, there were twelve thousand Śakras, Chief of Gods, as the leaders,
along with a great assembly of immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
They were all present in the assembly hall.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly,
who gazed upon him with reverence and listened to the Dharma with single-minded attention.
At that time, the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods was gathered in the Sudharmā Hall.
There was a certain devaputra named Sunetra,
who was riding in a great jewel-palace, attended by celestial maidens.
Surrounded by attendants before and behind, he indulged in unrestrained play and sport,
enjoying himself in the company of various courtesans. Then,
during the latter part of the night, he suddenly heard a voice in the air calling out:
"Devaputra Sunyati, from this day forward,
count seven days; you shall then relinquish your life-force and fall into Jambudvīpa to become seven kinds of animals."
Constantly consuming foul, evil, and impure things,
they subsequently fall into hell and undergo all manner of sufferings.
Only after many kalpas have passed do they finally obtain human form.
Although they obtain a human body, they are born without both eyes;
they are short, deformed, coarse, and ugly, with deficient sense faculties;
their breath is constantly foul, and they perpetually lack food and clothing.
"Poor, lowly, and despised by all—
such is the fate of one who is reviled.
When the devaputra Sunirmita heard these words, his heart was struck with alarm and terror.
With the hair on his entire body standing on end, he was filled with sorrow and distress.
He immediately prepared his palace with incense, flowers, and offerings,
and went to the abode of the Lord of Devas, where he knelt and prostrated at his feet.
Lamenting and weeping, he addressed the Lord of Devas, saying:
"Please listen to what I have to say. Within the Hall of Good Dharma, I was enjoying myself together with various celestial maidens and the assembly of devas."
Just as I was heading there, I suddenly heard a voice in the air calling out my name, saying:
"Seven days from now, the end of your life shall come; you will descend to be born in Jambudvīpa and undergo seven successive births in the bodies of animals."
They consume impure and filthy things as food,
and furthermore, they enter the hells to suffer for many kalpas;
later, when they obtain a human body, they are born without both eyes.
Their bodies were frail and emaciated, their appearance coarse and ugly;
their breath was foul and stinking, and they were poor, lowly, and base.
Bound by suffering and affliction, they were loathed by others.
"O Lord of Devas, how may I be delivered from this?
When Śakra heard these words,
he was greatly astonished and immediately reflected.
By what merit did the Devaputra Sunirmita previously attain birth in the heavens to experience such sublime bliss for so many kalpas?
And by what evil karma was his celestial retribution suddenly exhausted?
Within Jambudvīpa, they undergo the states of seven types of animals;
furthermore, entering into the hells, they fully experience manifold sufferings.
When born as humans, they are blind and possessed of every kind of evil.
At that time, Śakra, having reflected thus, further thought to himself: "What kind of animal body does this Sudhana possess?
He then observed his report with his divine eye.
In an instant, while in meditative concentration, he saw that Śubhavyūha was receiving seven types of animals—
namely, pigs, dogs, jackals, monkeys, pythons, snakes, crows, and vultures—
who constantly ate things of extreme foul odor and filth.
Having seen this, he was overcome with extreme distress;
his heart was pierced by grief and sorrow, and he felt such acute pain that he further thought:
"I have seen only a small portion of this retribution."
Furthermore, the causes that bring about profound and far-reaching matters are beyond my ability to fathom;
only the ocean of the Tathāgata’s perfect and universal knowledge can know such causes as those of good and evil.
I should go to consult the World-Honored One on this matter;
out of great compassion, the World-Honored One should explain the reason for it to us,
so that we may abide well and escape from this suffering.
At that time, Śakra immediately commanded the hosts of devas to each adorn their palaces and attendants with flower garlands,
necklaces, and various kinds of incense.
With powdered incense, burning incense, and celestial robes covering everything as an offering,
Śakra, accompanied by his retinue,
then swiftly came to the Jetavana Grove.
Having arrived, he made offerings;
having prostrated before the Buddha, he circumambulated him seven times to the right and then presented extensive offerings before the Buddha.
When the Dharma service was concluded, he stood to one side and,
receiving the Buddha’s holy command, addressed the World-Honored One:
"The Devaputra Sunetra, together with the celestial maidens and the host of devas..."
While he was sporting at will in the Hall of Good Dharma,
he suddenly heard a voice in the air proclaim:
"Seven days from now, the Devaputra Susthita shall pass away."
When their allotted destiny is exhausted, they receive the bodies of various animals;
entering hell, they fail to become human and undergo many sufferings as described above.
They reported this in full to the Buddha, saying:
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly and for our own sakes.
Regarding this Śubhavyūha, in a past life..."
By what meritorious deeds are they born in the heavens to experience pleasure for so many kalpas?
And by what causes and conditions do they, at the end of their lives,
fall away and become the seven kinds of animals mentioned above?
They take all manner of impurities as their food and drink,
and further enter the hells to undergo suffering for many kalpas;
even if they obtain a human body, it is stunted, ugly, and lowly.
He was blind, coarse, and ugly, shrouded by all manner of evils;
he was impoverished and foul-smelling, despised and cast aside by others.
Furthermore, what merit did he cultivate to evoke that voice from within the void to inform him of his retribution? Who was it that provided this causal condition?
We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Shan-zhu and those like us,
will explain the root of these causes, conditions, and retributions;
through his loving-kindness and mercy, may he rescue and deliver us so that we may attain liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra, saying:
"Good son, you possess a heart of great compassion;
you are able, for the sake of Suviṣṭhita, to inquire about the matters of the causes and conditions of the past, as well as the retributions of good and evil karma."
Furthermore, you have been able to entreat me to relieve you of your suffering.
This is most excellent, truly most excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively;
I shall now analyze and explain it for you.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance from the crown of his head,
which flowed and illuminated all Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions.
That light was five-colored— blue, red, yellow, white, and black— intermingling and reflecting one another as it whirled and turned to the right.
Returning to the place where the Buddha was, they circumambulated the Buddha three times and entered through the Buddha’s mouth.
Once the Buddha had withdrawn the light, he smiled.
He addressed Śakra, saying: "Listen attentively, listen attentively!

In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
After his parinirvāṇa, when his transformative work in the world was complete and the period of the Semblance Dharma had begun,
there was at that time a country named Vārāṇasī.
At that time, there was a brahmin who had only one son.
When the father passed away, his mother raised him alone.
As he gradually grew up, he went to the fields to cultivate the crops.
The poor mother went everywhere seeking food for him;
before she could find any, mealtime had already passed.
Her son, tormented by hunger and thirst, gave rise to a mind of anger and resentment toward his mother.
He immediately uttered harsh words: "For what reason has she not come today to bring food?
She has vexed me with resentment and malice, returning again and again.
He then spoke these words of rage: "My mother now is no better than a beast."
I have seen swine, dogs, jackals, monkeys, crows, vultures, and the like who,
out of affection for their offspring,
do not allow them to suffer from hunger or thirst and never abandon them for even a moment.
"Why does my mother not come to see me?
Why does she not send food even though I am so hungry and thirsty?
While harboring such resentment for no long time, [he passed away].
The mother, having sought out food, quickly brought it there;
she comforted her son and made him joyful.
Just as he sat down, wishing to eat, [the food vanished].
Suddenly, he saw in the sky a Pratyekabuddha in the form of a śramaṇa,
flying from the south and soaring through the air toward the north.
Upon seeing him, the son felt a sense of reverence and admiration arise within his heart.
He immediately rose, joined his palms, and prostrated himself with his head at [the other's] feet,
inviting him to deign to visit.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha accepted his invitation.
His son, filled with joy, spread a seat of white *māṛa* grass,
offered pure and exquisite flowers, and set aside a portion of his own food,
which he brought to present to the bhikṣu. Having thus provided the meal, [he departed].
He taught him the essentials of the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting,
and gladdening him. Later, the son again went forth as a monk and was appointed to the office of *karmadāna* (steward).
At that time, there was a brahmin who constructed a monastery and settled his disciples there.
Furthermore, a donor sent a large quantity of ghee and oil.
At that time, various visiting monks were eating in the monastery.
When the *karmadāna* saw this, his mind became stingy and filled with anger;
he resented the guests and caused them distress, refusing to give them any food, such as ghee or oil.
A visiting monk asked, "This is a gift from a donor intended for the *saṃgha* present here."
For what reason did he remain there instead of leading the assembly?
It was because that *karmadāna* was impetuous and of a wicked disposition;
he immediately began to shout insults at the visiting monks.
"Why do you eat excrement and urine while seeking butter?
Are your eyes blind?
Do you think I would hide the butter from you when you see it?"
The Buddha told Śakra:
"The brahmin's son at that time was none other than the present-day Devaputra Sunirmita.
It was because of those angry words that he was led to compare his mother to a beast."
Now, having been summoned seven times to take birth in the bodies of animals,
and furthermore, because he uttered foul words while serving as a *vaitālika* (court bard),
his karma causes him to constantly consume impurities.
Because he was stingy regarding the food of the Sangha, he suffered in hell;
because he reviled those who were blind, he received the retribution of being sightless,
remaining without both eyes for seven hundred lifetimes.
They shall dwell for a long time in darkness and undergo great suffering.
O Lord of Devas, you should know that such karmic offenses will inevitably bring their retribution; they shall never perish without being experienced.
Furthermore, O Lord of Devas, as for the noble son Sudṛṣṭa who has attained birth in the heavens,
it is due to the power of his past offerings to pratyekabuddhas—
spreading seats, offering flowers, reverently bestowing food, and hearing the Dharma.
Now, having received celestial blessings, he shall experience constant, supreme, and wondrous joy for as many kalpas as those enumerated.
Furthermore, when a pratyekabuddha flies through the air,
that person resolves his mind by gazing upward toward the sky.
With a devoted heart, he paid homage by prostrating himself with his head at the ground.
By virtue of this merit, he now relies upon the divine voice from the sky to receive a prior notification;
the one who provides this notification is the Guardian Spirit of the Hall, Susthitavihārin.
At that time, Suvikrāntaśīla, having received what the Buddha had taught,
immediately understood that his own karma was entirely due to past conditions.
He then deeply reproached himself before the Buddha.
Due to my past anger toward my mother, my resentment toward the Sangha, my harsh abuse, and my stinginess and greed,
I have incurred this great transgression in the future.
Now, receiving Your Holiness’s instruction, I shall repent with all my life.
He threw his entire body prostrate upon the ground;
his whole frame was covered in clotted blood like a squeezed flower-sack,
and after remaining unconscious for a long while, he gradually regained consciousness.
They wailed and wept with rain-like tears, their grief beyond measure.
The Buddha told Śubhavyūha and Śakra, Lord of Devas:
"Among the conditions of the ten non-virtuous actions, harsh speech is the most grievous."
One should know that harsh abuse is more severe than a fierce fire;
for while such a fire merely burns wealth of the seven treasures and merely consumes worldly objects of enjoyment and play, [abuse consumes something far more profound].
The fierce fire of harsh speech can burn away the seven treasures of the noble ones;
it can incinerate all supramundane merits,
utterly extinguishing them and swiftly summoning an evil retribution.
As you have dwelled well in these words— once resenting your mother and once reviling the Sangha—
your heavenly retribution will be exhausted and you shall again enter hell.
One should not disparage or revile the Heavenly Emperor, one's parents, or the Sangha;
rather, it is right to respect, revere, and make offerings to them.
One should speak to them with gentle words, praise them, and constantly be mindful of their kindness.
Within the three realms, parents alone possess loving-kindness;
among the fields of merit throughout the three periods of time, none surpasses the Sangha—
such as the eightfold assembly of true monks and the twelve classes of noble sages.
Those who make offerings do not fail to gain merit;
those who seek transcendence can advance toward the realization of the Way.
How could one ever dare to utter deceitful words within the Sangha?
Parents undergo toil and hardship in giving birth and raising their children.
They carry them in the womb for ten months and nurse them for three years;
in nurturing and instructing them, they exhaust every measure of difficulty and anxiety.
I hope that he will achieve success and excel in his talents beyond others;
furthermore, I wish for him to leave the household life and transcend birth and death.
Because of these thoughts of gratitude, the debt is as vast as heaven and difficult to repay.
Therefore, I said to Ānanda:
"Carry your father on your left shoulder and your mother on your right shoulder,
and circumambulate Mount Sumeru a hundred thousand times."
Even if blood flowed until it submerged one's ankles, one could not repay the kindness of being nursed for a single day;
how much less should one harbor evil thoughts, seek to end one's life, or utter words of resentment.
The Buddha told Śakra Devendra and the Devaputra Sunvāsa:
"Because you have now seen me, you shall attain the purity of the five eyes.
Because your repentance is thorough, your transgressions shall likewise be extinguished.
The Buddha looked toward Śubhavyūha and said to him:
Cease your weeping; I have a dharma gate called the Most Victorious Uṣṇīṣa Dhāraṇī Mantra.
One who upholds this mantra shall be able to cause you to leave suffering behind and attain liberation.
Abide well in this most supreme Buddha-uṣṇīṣa dhāraṇī mantra;
it has been spoken by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of koṭis of Buddhas.
I shall now recite this dhāraṇī mantra.
It is the most honored and supreme among all Buddha-uṣṇīṣas;
it can extinguish all karmic obstructions and cause them to be entirely purified;
it can extract beings from the realms of hell, animals, and Yama.
It can eliminate all the suffering and affliction of birth and death for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, he addressed the Lord of Devas:
"This pure Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Supreme Dhāraṇī Mantra—if there are good men or good women, bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs..."
If one who is able to receive and uphold this [text] either reads or recites it,
by virtue of these merits, the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes shall all be extinguished throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
They immediately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Without changing this body, they obtain the knowledge of past lives and pass from one buddha-field to another buddha-field.
May they always receive the blessing of the crowning touch and the extending hand from Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara,
and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and receive the prediction of their future attainment of Bodhisattvahood;
may they always remain within the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), hearing and upholding the True Dharma.
Having attained omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), their lifespan is further increased;
their body, speech, and mind are pure, and they do not meet with untimely death.
They are fully endowed with wholesome contact, and their entire being is sublime and excellent.
At all times and in all places, one will swiftly attain pliancy.
If, at the time of death, one recites this dhāraṇī,
one will immediately attain rebirth in the lands of the various Buddhas.
At that time, Śakra, hearing the Buddha praise the inconceivable merit of this most supreme dhāraṇī,
was filled with deep joy and longing, and with a single-minded devotion,
he addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "I pray only that the Tathāgata..."
Out of compassion for Shan-zhu and those like us,
as well as for sentient beings of the future age of dharma decline,
please preach this most supreme Buddha-uṣṇīṣa dhāraṇī mantra.
"I shall practice so as to cause all sentient beings to forever leave behind the suffering of the eight difficulties.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this mantra for the sake of Śakra, the Deva-king, the son of a god named Susthita, and the fourfold assembly: [Mantra follows]
Namo bhagavate trailokyaprativiśiṣṭāya buddhāya bhagavate.
Tadyathā. Oṃ viśuddhaya samantāvabhāsa.
6. Śavarana-ghati-gahana-svābhu (7) Abhiṣeñca-sugata-vajra (8) Avatīrta-piśāce (9) Aha-ra aha-ra (10) Ā-yus-manta.
1. Rāṇi 2. Śuddhaye śuddhaye 3. Gaganaviśuddhe 4. Uṣṇīṣavijayaśuddhe 5.
Sahasraraśmi-sañcodite 6. Sarvadharmatejovikrāmiṇe svāhā.
Vajra-ākarṣaya saṃharaṇa-āveśaya sarva-varaṇa-viśodhaya pratyarthika-nirghātaya āyur-viśodhaya samayādhiṣṭhitāḥ. (16–20)
Maṇi maṇi (21) | tathāgata-koṭi-pariśuddhi (22) | viśvabhūti-śuddhi (23) | śāye śāye (24) | viśāye viśāye (25) | samara samara buddha-adhiṣṭhe (26) ||
Tastuti (26) Vajravidāriṇi (27) Vajrapramardani (28) Māmaki (29) Sarvasattvopajīvya (30) Sarvatathāgataparishuddhi (31) Sarva...
[The text continues with the mantra syllables.]
Tathāgata-samavasaraṇa-āśrite (31) buddhabuddha (32) samantapariśuddhe sarvatathāgatādhiṣṭhāna (33) (Note:
*Samavasaraṇa* is pronounced with a *va* sound; *āśrite* has a long vowel;
*buddha* is repeated; *pariśuddhe* has a long vowel; *adhiṣṭhāna* has a long vowel.)
*Ādhiṣṭhe mahāmudre svāhā.* The Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"This is my *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-dhāraṇī-mantra*, the most supreme among all pure destinies."
This dhāraṇī mantra is capable of purifying all obstacles such as sinful karma and is capable of purifying all sufferings of the three evil realms;
it was proclaimed together by eighty-eight koṭis of Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
It is solemnly recorded, protected, rejoiced in, and praised;
it is collectively endorsed by all Tathāgatas,
for it is able to purify and eliminate the ten evil transgressions of all sentient beings.
Because it is able to rescue all those in the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and Yama;
and because if the meritorious karma of all sentient beings gradually diminishes,
they would otherwise be subject to short lifespans, chronic illness, and ugliness.
Those who are physically impaired, impoverished, low-born, blind, deaf, or mute,
and who ought to fall into the realms of hell or animals to undergo various sufferings and afflictions—
if they hear me recite the name of this dhāraṇī— [they shall be liberated].
When the retribution for evil is extinguished, one attains liberation.
If there are sentient beings who have accumulated evil karma—
the ten non-virtuous actions, the five heinous crimes, and all such karmic obstructions— [they shall likewise be purified].
Whether light or heavy, all shall be completely extinguished;
one shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and forever be free from all suffering and hardship.
They shall forever be free from all rebirths among animals and in the realm of Yama;
furthermore, they shall attain complete liberation from all such realms as those of the asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, and apasmārakas.
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas: "If there should be anyone who is able to receive and uphold this mantra,
from the time they have received and upheld it onward, they shall forever be free from the evil realms and shall always dwell in the same place as the Buddhas of the ten directions."
Among the supreme companions of the Bodhisattva Ever-Constant,
he may take birth within noble Brahmin lineages,
always remaining in the sites of enlightenment and the pure lands of all Buddhas.
"Up until the attainment of unsurpassed bodhi,
one shall obtain the liberation-body of the Tathāgata’s ocean of perfect and universal knowledge.
The Buddha then addressed Śakra, Lord of Devas, and the Prince Sudhīra.
This *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-dhāraṇī-mantra* of mine, which purifies all realms of existence and is most supreme,
possesses vast majesty and great merit, and wields mighty power;
it is like an auspicious day and like a mani jewel.
Brilliantly pure and stainless as the void,
wherever it is present, its radiance illuminates the world,
like the most supreme of the seven jewels in the world.
All sentient beings— including kings, princes, royal mothers, high officials, and ministers— as well as anyone who beholds them,
will collectively hold them in high esteem and take delight in seeing them without ever growing weary.
Because these sublime jewels cannot be defiled by impurities,
O Lord of Devas, this dhāraṇī is likewise. If there is anyone who receives,
maintains, recites, copies, or makes offerings to it, that person [shall be protected].

By virtue of these merits, they are likewise held in high esteem by all the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings, who do not wish to relinquish them for even a moment, as if they were those wondrous jewels. Why is this?
It is because of the power of this dhāraṇī.
Because it can cause all the heavy sins of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts to be completely extinguished;
furthermore, by the power of this dhāraṇī.
Because it enables those who uphold it to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha told Śakra Devendra and the devaputra Sudhīra:
"If there should be a king, a prince, a queen mother, a crown prince, or any of the hundred officials or ministers..."
Furthermore, for the sake of making offerings, monks, nuns, sons of good family, daughters of good family,
and others shall write down this dhāraṇī mantra and place it within a stūpa made of the seven precious gems.
Either upon a precious lion throne,
or within a vajra pedestal,
or inside a stūpa containing relics.
If there are beings of the four modes of birth atop a high banner,
or if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās;
Having committed the ten non-virtuous actions, the five crimes of immediate retribution,
the four grave prohibitions, and all other serious offenses,
they ought to be reborn in the realm of Yama or suffer in any of the six destinies according to their respective karmic conditions.
If these sinful persons pass to and fro near this stūpa of the dhāraṇī,
and even a single mote of dust from the stūpa falls upon their bodies,
all the aforementioned sins shall be completely extinguished.
If the wind passes by and blows upon those stupas and the like,
and further touches even a small portion of a person's body,
that person will immediately be reborn in heaven to experience supreme and wondrous bliss.
Furthermore, one may be reborn in the Pure Land according to one's own wishes.
If there is anyone who upholds this dhāraṇī,
when they wish to wash their hands and pour water over their palms, [the following occurs].
When that water falls to the ground, it sprinkles upon insects and ants;
these various creatures immediately attain rebirth in heaven.
Therefore, whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, or men and women—
If there is one who can maintain the fast and precepts with purity during the six periods of the day and night,
and without fail uphold this dhāraṇī mantra,
all the roots of the five heinous crimes, the four grave offenses, and the ten evil deeds committed throughout the three periods of time by that person [shall be extinguished].
All their grave offenses shall be completely extinguished.
For the sake of all bodhisattvas and all Tathāgatas,
[the Buddhas] will stroke their heads with their own hands, bestow upon them the prophecy of their attainment of bodhisattvahood, and address them, saying:
"Good son, you who are able to receive and uphold this most supreme Buddha-uṣṇīṣa dhāraṇī mantra shall,
in a future life, certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:
"If there should be someone who is able to construct various jeweled stūpas at a crossroads, or erect a tall banner and install this dhāraṇī sūtra therein."
Furthermore, by making offerings of various kinds of flowers, incense, garlands, ornaments made of the seven treasures, exquisite garments, food, drink, and medicinal decoctions,
the merit of such a person shall be immeasurable and boundless.
The merit and wisdom of such a person are beyond measure and calculation.
Such a person is indeed a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva;
such a person is truly a son of the Buddha.
Why is this? Because it delivers immeasurable sentient beings who come and go beneath the stupa.
At that time, King Yama, the Dharma King...
Then, during the latter part of that very night,
he took his retinue of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions,
carrying various fragrant flowers and diverse ornaments.
They came to where the Buddha was and presented offerings to him;
they circumambulated him seven times to the right, prostrated at his feet,
and made offerings with various flowers and incense.
He addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas: "If there are sentient beings with short lifespans who seek long life..."
